title: What should the next call remember?

beats.say: Follow this callback through the incident recorder. Request R seventeen returned four oh three. Someone penciled in a cause, a database lock, and proposed a rollback.

Slide the lock check under the trace. Line up request R seventeen on both strips, then time one hundred. Read the lock detector at that instant. Would you carry the penciled explanation into the next call?
Erase the guess. The detector saw no migration lock for R seventeen at time one hundred. Clip the source ID to that finding. We still need to find out why the callback failed.

Assemble the next call around that question. Send the investigation instructions, the trace lookup tool, the trace, and the checked note. Leave the old guess and the recaps that repeat it in the archive. The pieces you send are the model’s working set.

title: Where did the evidence land?

beats.say: Suppose the input limit is a hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens. This investigation fits. A trimmer that waits until the window is full has no reason to touch it. Yet a request can keep the old lock explanation or leave out the record that would correct it. Build for the question before the window fills.

Even a record that makes it into the request can be hard to use. In Lost in the Middle, models answering multi-document questions or looking up a value often did better with the evidence near either end. Chroma’s twenty twenty-five study tested eighteen models.
Longer inputs and similar distractors often made retrieval harder. Those experiments give us a reason to move our own evidence and test again.

Ask for the status in trace seventeen. Move the same record from the beginning through the middle to the end. Keep the question, the text and the answer key fixed. Now ask a different question. Could a scope change explain the callback failure?

One record shows where the request failed. The other shows what the deployment changed. We’d have to check which scope the callback needed before blaming that change. Score this two-source question separately. When reporting a needle benchmark, name the variant. Some require several facts.

For a supplied twelve-case probe, ten successes at the beginning mean eighty-three and one third percent. Seven in the middle mean fifty-eight and one third percent. Subtract the success fractions and multiply by one hundred to obtain a twenty-five percentage-point change.

Score the questions that need both records separately. For example, if five of eight two-source questions pass, report five out of eight, or sixty-two and a half percent. Keep the model and the probe with those scores.

title: Different symptoms require different edits to the same packet

beats.say: A wrong lock claim repeatedly cited as fact is poisoning. Re-running old failed searches instead of checking a new trace is distraction. Selecting an inappropriate administrative tool from overlapping descriptions is confusion. A retrieved instruction demanding XML while the application requires JSON is a clash.
Take the lock guess and the XML instruction first. Which belongs outside the active request entirely? Which can stay if we mark where it came from?

For poisoning, remove the false claim and summaries derived from it before the next plan. Retain the checked negative finding with its source and observation window. For distraction, select the new evidence instead of replaying the same low-value search history. An added apology alone can leave the original false span inside the next request.

For confusion, narrow the tool schemas to the current phase. For clash, preserve the retrieved passage as untrusted evidence without promoting its formatting instruction into policy. An XML example quoted as data need not conflict with a JSON output contract.
Change one assembly choice at a time, then compare matched tasks and the full resulting traces.

title: Store a finding, then reload what is useful

beats.say: Open the callback trace and the lock observation. The trace shows an HTTP four oh three on the callback. The lock detector reports no migration lock for the same request at the same time. We can save both observations. We still have an open question about the cause.

Write both findings with their source IDs into a separate note store. Serialize the records and read them back. The source IDs survive that round trip. A later investigator who needs more detail can still open the original trace.

Reloading a note puts its tokens back into the model's input. External storage helps because the application chooses what to read, while the complete archive can remain outside this call. Preserve observation time, source revision, and uncertainty so a later session knows what must be rechecked.

title: A stored note carries scope and a verifier result

beats.say: Look at the three values for confirmed. One is a string in quotes. One is the number one. One is a Boolean. Which type can this field accept? The function rejects the first two. Only the host can set the Boolean to true after checking the source.

Record the source revision, trace identity, observation time, status and uncertainty beside a finding. No lock during the inspected transaction is narrower than no lock ever. A later source revision can require a new check. Reload only the needed note, while keeping a path back to the complete archived observation.

Writing saves information outside the active call. A file, a database or a thread checkpoint can hold the note for the next shift. Before loading it, check that the caller may read it, the source is current and the finding answers this question. The reloaded words count toward the next call’s input.

title: Expose the tools for the current phase

beats.say: During investigation, the next useful actions read deployment records and trace spans. The phase policy intersects those tool identities with the tools actually available. Their schemas enter the prompt, while unrelated administrative choices remain outside this step's working set.

A later proposal phase needs a different set. Watch the same tool identities change eligibility when the phase changes. Progressive disclosure reduces irrelevant choices and schema tokens. It also makes the intended workflow visible enough to test with concrete requests.

An unknown phase exposes no tools in this fixture. Execution authorization still belongs at the tool boundary, where identity and permissions must be checked on every call. Hiding a schema organizes model context. The backend must also reject actions that the caller is not allowed to perform.

title: Construct the complete article tool intersection

beats.say: Here is the article's larger investigation policy. Alongside deploy lookup and trace lookup it allows runbook search. A schema enters the request when its ID is both allowed and available. Compare all five sockets. Read the three connected tools in sorted order.

Switch to proposal mode on the same catalog. Runbook search and rollback advisor are eligible; the other schemas leave the prompt. An unknown phase maps to the empty set. If trace lookup is unavailable during investigation, intersection removes it without granting a replacement tool. The result follows identity membership, rather than a guessed tool count.

Prompt visibility and execution permission are separate tests. Even a tool omitted from the prompt can be named in a malformed or hostile attempted call. The backend checks caller identity, current scope and action permissions on every attempt. Selecting fewer schemas can reduce irrelevant choices and token use, but those effects still require task evaluation.

title: Move the changing header behind the reusable prefix

beats.say: During prefill, the model processes the input and builds attention keys and values. On a compatible cache hit, the server can reuse the saved states for the matching start of the request. It processes the remaining input, then decodes the output.
A changed early timestamp can block reuse of stable material after it without deleting an older cache entry.

Lay the two requests on the same token ruler. Each has a ninety-six-token root, a twelve-token header and a two-hundred-fifty-six-token document. The headers start with different tokens. With every boundary eligible, where does the match stop?

The first match stops at ninety-six. Slide the changing header behind the fixed document on both requests. Read the ruler again. Now the common prefix is three hundred fifty-two tokens. Each complete request still contains three hundred sixty-four.

The root and document now match across requests. Hash the rendered prefix bytes locally to check that match. Read the provider's cached input count and measure latency to see what work it reused. Routing, eviction or expiry can turn a match into a miss.
Keep this phase’s tools first, the fixed document next, and the changing notes last. When the phase changes, update the tools too.

title: Caching changes repeated work while the same input still occupies capacity

beats.say: Cached tokens still occupy logical input capacity and remain available to attention. A perfectly cached long history can still contain a misleading claim. Curation tests whether the retained evidence supports the decision; cache measurements test reuse and serving cost.
Neither measurement replaces the other, and necessary evidence should not be discarded to improve a cache-hit percentage.

Use the selected provider’s actual accounting for cache writes, cache reads, uncached input and output, including applicable request modifiers. Some cache writes cost more than ordinary input. Separate cache groups can organize routing or billing and reduce cross-user cache-hit probing where supported. They do not authorize which user’s document enters the request.

Before constructing even a likely cache hit, check the caller’s identity and access scope. Pin the model, tokenizer, request serialization and relevant tool definitions when measuring reuse. Keep cache metrics beside task quality, input and output usage, end-to-end latency and total cost.

Now take the same request on a route with an empty cache. The cached input count drops to zero. All three hundred sixty-four input tokens still fit, and the evidence is identical. A miss can reflect routing, changed tokens, eviction or expiry.

title: Remove bulk while retaining checked state

beats.say: Read the six lengths in this packet. The gray export holds eighty-two hundred assigned units. Two source-linked findings preserve what we have checked so far. Which single piece could we take out without losing the way back to the original observations?

Prune the bulky raw export after preserving its checked findings and source references. The active packet becomes much smaller. Keep valid call and result identities when reconstructing a real transcript, and retain recent output whose meaning has not yet been captured in a verified note.

Exclude tools outside the phase and remove the disproven claim. Reloaded findings still count in the remaining input, which the ledger shows explicitly. The smaller result is a candidate working set. Its usefulness depends on whether it preserves what the task requires, so quality evaluation follows the accounting.

title: Replace only old output whose finding is already preserved

beats.say: Read the four results in order. The function keeps the latest two raw. It subtracts that number from the result count and clamps the cutoff at zero. Look before that boundary for an older result whose finding-recorded flag is the exact Boolean true. Which payload can we replace?

Take four ordered results and keep the most recent two. The cutoff is index two. If the flags are true, false, true, true, only index zero is replaced. Index one remains because its finding is unrecorded. Indices two and three remain because they are recent.
This rule preserves unresolved detail rather than compressing every old response automatically.

The article returns replacement strings as a content illustration. A real provider transcript must preserve valid tool-call and tool-result identifiers, order and message structure. Bound raw output at ingress, archive it before pruning, and retain exact error text or identifiers needed by the next check.
Measure finalized requests instead of treating these strings as provider messages.

title: Compression must preserve uncertainty and pending external state

beats.say: A useful summary records observations, hypotheses, rejected possibilities, source identities, unresolved questions and next checks. Authentication suspected is different from authentication confirmed as the cause. Keep negative findings with their time window. LLMLingua uses a smaller model to shorten the prompt to a token budget.

Read the two observations for request R seventeen at time one hundred. Trace seventeen records the callback’s four oh three. The lock check rules out a lock at that instant. What would you still have to check before calling the scope change the cause?

Compare the scope the callback required with the scope the deployment granted to this request. Until you check those permissions, the scope change stays a hypothesis. Summarization can carry an injected instruction into later memory. Label the summary as source-derived history, preserve its provenance, and keep policy authority separate. A generated field named verified has meaning only through the host check that set it. Neither a summary nor a retrieved procedure can grant new tool permissions.

Suppose an approved rollback request went out and its reply never arrived. Save the exact payload, operation key and last confirmed result. Mark the outcome unknown. Ask the service about that key before deciding whether to retry. The summary can point the next shift to this execution record.

title: What comes back from the search?

beats.say: Suppose a worker inspects fifty commits for a change that might explain the callback failure. Each mark is a commit the worker inspected. The lead has its own conversation. All it needs from this search is a finding it can check.
In this small example, the reply has just two fields, claim and source, and a two hundred byte limit.

The worker reports a callback failure and cites trace seventeen. Open that source in the caller’s authorized archive. The callback returned four oh three, so a failure is supported. Copy the finding and source together. The commit history stays in the worker window. Count both windows and enforce read permissions for each worker.
Try the same claim with a missing source ID. The receiver checks the set of records this caller may read. There’s no record to open. The lead gets no finding from this attempt.

For the third try, the worker cites the real trace but says the request succeeded. Open trace seventeen again. Four oh three contradicts that success claim. Leave it out of the lead’s note. A separate window lets us leave search history behind. The application still controls file access and tool execution.

title: What can the lead accept from the worker?

beats.say: Let’s use the full handoff contract. The receiver allows sixteen hundred bytes. Here’s a JSON object with spaces after its closing brace. Every space counts on the wire. The last one is byte fifteen ninety-nine. Add two more spaces. Will the receiver open this copy?

It stops at sixteen hundred and one bytes. The receiver checks length before it decodes UTF-eight or parses JSON. Bound the read at the transport too, so an oversized reply can’t consume unbounded memory before this check. A character can take several bytes.

Take the two spaces back off. Now the receiver can open the original. It rejects malformed UTF-eight and duplicate JSON keys. These three fields are the whole contract. The claim and next check each need nonempty text.
The source list needs at least one ID, and every ID must belong to the caller’s authorized set. An extra field or a wrong type fails the check.
The worker says HTTP two hundred. Its source ID passed. Open the cited trace. Compare the two status codes. Can the lead record two hundred for this request?

Withhold that claim. The trace says four oh three. Change just the worker’s status to four oh three. The envelope is still fifteen ninety-nine bytes. This time the values match. Keep the status and the trace ID together. The lead can now open that trace to investigate the failed callback.

Count the worker’s input and output as well as the lead’s, and measure the time the lead waited. A smaller lead request can still mean more total work. Check which records each process or remote provider could see.

title: Reconstruct all retained allocation terms

beats.say: Now expand the allocation behind the earlier compression picture. Task and evidence use twenty-four hundred assigned units. Scratchpad and active tools use seven hundred sixty. Two reloaded findings use ninety plus ninety-six, or one hundred eighty-six. Those retained groups total three thousand three hundred forty-six.

Now weigh what left the call. The export uses eighty-two hundred, unused schemas seven hundred seventy, and the old guess one hundred twenty. Together that is nine thousand ninety. To find the fraction omitted, divide by the original input size. What number goes in that denominator?
Adding retained and removed groups reconstructs twelve thousand four hundred thirty-six, with seventy-three point one percent omitted after rounding.

We chose what to keep and assigned the sizes. Most of the saving comes from leaving the old trace export in the archive. For a real call, count the finished messages and tool schemas with the model’s tokenizer. Include reloaded notes and cached input. Then try answering the same question from the shorter request.

title: Place protected evidence before optional material

beats.say: First check the inputs. The budget and sizes must be nonnegative integers. A Boolean size fails. Each item needs an integer priority, a Boolean required flag and a unique nonempty name. Sort required items first, then higher priorities. Keep ties in their original order. Try each item against the space still available.

With a three-thousand-unit allocation, the required alert and trace use six hundred. The optional runbook brings use to twenty-four hundred. The export does not fit. Start another run and make the full dump required. Required items go first. Even before the optional runbook, the alert, trace and dump would use eighty-eight hundred. Stop before sending.

Reserve instructions, message and tool framing, and output or reasoning allowance before choosing this allocation. For a supplied total of four thousand ninety-six, reserves of four hundred twenty, one hundred eighty and one thousand twenty-four leave twenty-four hundred seventy-two. The same twenty-four-hundred-unit selected set leaves seventy-two units unused.

title: Who owns the failing callback?

beats.say: Who owns the failing callback? We have six hundred units left. The error log ranks first and fills the budget. It gives us the status code. Try the route map and the service directory instead. Each costs three hundred units. Follow the callback through those two records. Which team gets the page?

Page the Access team. The route map takes us from the callback to Identity. The directory tells us who owns Identity. Bundle the map and directory so the packer keeps both links. What counts as required depends on the question. A rollback runbook can be optional during diagnosis and required when proposing a rollback.

Suppose the budget drops to five hundred units. Both records are required, so stop before sending the request. Extract the two entries you need, split the task into two lookups, or report which evidence is missing. Check access before selecting either record. Then count the finished request and see whether it answers the ownership question.

title: Count context work against completed task steps

beats.say: Context bloat is the old material piling up. Watch what happens when the summary drops the request ID. Fetch the trace, summarize it, drop the original, fetch the same trace again, and summarize it again. Five context operations and zero completed task steps. That loop is thrashing.
With zero completed steps, the ratio is undefined. Write down both counts and mark this run stalled. A made-up denominator would make a stalled task look productive.

Track operations per completed step where defined, repeated-span reloads, evidence yield and decision latency. A valid search can return no result, so do not require an invented confirmed fact after every call. A ruled-out path or a precisely identified evidence gap can still advance the investigation.

Pin a required request ID until its job is finished or freshness requires a new read. Cap retries and preparation work. Once that budget is exhausted, preserve the state and report the missing evidence or escalate. Reducing churn should not convert an unknown external outcome into a successful one or repeat an unconfirmed write.

title: Load metadata, one procedure and only the needed resource

beats.say: An Agent Skill packages a required SKILL dot M D file with a name and description in its frontmatter, plus optional references, scripts and assets. Discovery exposes the name and trigger description. The specification’s roughly one hundred metadata tokens and below-five-thousand-body recommendation are guidance, not actual tokenizer counts for every skill.

On activation, load the chosen procedure body. Read a reference only when its details are needed. In Anthropic’s documented execution setup, a script can run without its source entering model context; its returned output still enters. Other runtimes may expose different material, so count what this runtime actually sends.

Now count the prompt. Six labels at eighty units each give four hundred eighty. Add one activated body of twenty-two hundred, a four-hundred-unit reference and one hundred twenty units of returned output. That comes to three thousand two hundred assigned units. The script source and the other five bodies stay on disk.

title: Test activation, artifact production and authority separately

beats.say: Read the incident skill’s description. It covers failed deployments, traces and evidence handoffs. A canary investigation opens the skill. A vacation-policy summary leaves it unloaded. A request to roll back a failed deployment also matches. Follow that last request.

The router selects incident triage. Its script returns a rollback proposal. The attached finding says the callback returned four oh three and cites trace seventeen. The validator opens that trace. The two status codes match, so it accepts the finding. Now read the skill’s permissions. It can read records. What would it need to change the deployment?

A rollback requires a write. The host denies the write. The proposal stays on file for the incident lead to review. Before installing a skill, review its publisher, instructions and scripts. Keep short instructions that every call needs in the stable base. Load the incident procedure when its trigger matches. Count missed and mistaken activations, measure the tokens sent, and check how much work it takes to return a usable handoff.

title: Bind a resume receipt to its actual inputs

beats.say: A later session needs to know which work remains valid. The trusted receipt in this fixture binds a checked artifact to its input revision. Recompute both hashes before resuming. An unchanged artifact and matching input set let the harness select the next dependent task.
Change the deployment input from revision seven to revision eight. Leave the report in place. Compare its two fingerprints, then compare the input pair. Can the next task rely on the old receipt?

The input check fails. The receipt belongs to revision seven. Now restore the input and change the artifact itself. The report hash fails instead. A trusted receipt establishes byte consistency under its manifest. Evidence quality, evaluator identity, freshness and execution authority each need their own checks.

title: Reconstruct five durable objects before choosing work

beats.say: This restart uses five artifacts. The task manifest lists unique IDs, dependencies and acceptance criteria. The progress log records attempts, errors and findings. A bootstrap command checks the environment. A work receipt binds results to artifact and input bytes, acceptance version and evaluator. The recovery rule defines timeouts, retries and escalation.

After a restart, the progress log can tell you where the last shift stopped. The work receipt tells you which result you can reuse. A framework such as LangGraph can save a thread in a checkpoint and share records across threads through a store.
Your application chooses which records to reload and checks the receipt before continuing.

Our graph collects traces, verifies cause, then writes a report. Only collect traces is initially done with a valid trusted receipt. The next ready task is verify cause. A progress note saying all done cannot advance the graph. Recompute acceptance evidence before choosing the next dependent task.

title: Validate the entire graph and exact receipt contract

beats.say: Validate the graph before trusting done labels. Reject empty or duplicate IDs, invalid status, missing or repeated dependency IDs and cycles, including cycles among tasks labeled done. A done task must have a receipt and every dependency must also be verified done.
Among pending tasks, select the first whose dependencies are all in that verified set.

The receipt must name the same task, the expected evaluator and contract version, and passed must be the actual Boolean true. Recompute the artifact digest and every declared input digest. Require exact equality between the manifest input set and receipt input keys.

Now the manifest also requires the approval policy. The receipt has no entry for that file. The harness stops even though every digest already present still matches. A verifier must check the extra input before the dependent task can start.

Use relative paths inside the checkpoint directory. Reject a path that resolves outside it. This check assumes the files stay in place while you read them. If other processes can change them, enforce that boundary when opening the file.
With a trusted receipt, matching hashes tell you the files still hold the bytes the evaluator checked.

title: A restart must preserve execution uncertainty and independent checks

beats.say: The investigator’s draft blames a migration lock for the failed callback, cites trace seventeen, and proposes a rollback. A schema check verifies that the report has the required fields. A separate evaluator checks each causal claim against the records and looks for alternative explanations. Read the trace beside the lock check. Which line of the draft would you change?

Both records name R seventeen at time one hundred. The trace shows four oh three. The detector found no migration lock. The evaluator removes the lock claim. It keeps the detector’s finding and its source. The cause is still open. Compare the scope the callback needed with the scope the deployment granted. Rollback stays a proposal. The incident lead would have to approve it.

A write went out under operation key K seventeen. Its response was lost. Ask the resource about that key. Sending the same key again must not trigger a second effect. Now a worker presents fencing token eleven when the resource has accepted twelve. The resource rejects the stale writer. A lease recorded only in the prompt could never enforce that check.

Restrict who can issue receipts and change task status. Append-only storage can retain history but still allow a forged new entry if writers are untrusted. Recheck live state when freshness matters. A resumable summary is useful orientation; trustworthy continuation requires the actual state, evidence and resource-bound execution rules.

title: Protect the cases that the average can hide

beats.say: Test curation with paired tasks. Our deterministic reader can answer a question only when its required source is present. The baseline packet supplies four of the six answers. This miniature test makes evidence coverage inspectable while leaving language-model reasoning quality for a separate evaluation.

The candidate packet supplies five answers, improving the aggregate. Look at which row changed, though. It omitted the source that states who authorizes a rollback. A more successful average can coexist with losing a fact that the workflow must always preserve.

Apply the protected-case requirement and the candidate is rejected. The result follows from actual source lookup and comparison with expected answers. A production suite should also inspect claim support, malicious instructions, model variation, latency, and cost on the same cases before promoting a new curation policy.

title: Would you ship the shorter request?

beats.say: Now try ten paired incident cases. These are invented outcomes. Each column is the same case run with two inputs. The shorter input uses three thousand three hundred forty-six assigned units. Read the curated row. Two cases improve and one regresses.
Correct answers rise from seven to eight. The yellow mark is a promise we made before testing. Case two has to pass. Would you ship this version?

Hold it at case two. The gate requires fewer input units, at least as many successes overall, a pass on every protected case, and zero poisoning events. The other three conditions hold. In a fresh retest, change just case two from fail to pass.
Keep every other result and both input sizes fixed. Does the candidate pass this suite now?

Yes. Nine cases pass, including the protected case. The release rule now accepts the candidate for this suite. The rule needs at least one case and positive integer token counts. The outcomes and protected flags must be Booleans. Poisoning counts must be nonnegative integers.

For a real policy change, repeat the comparison on matched tasks with recorded model and policy versions. Include buried clues, similar incident IDs, unsupported claims and unauthorized requests. Keep answer quality, worker usage, latency and total cost beside the input counts.

title: Can you get back to the trace?

beats.say: Here are two callback records. Both could produce the sentence, the callback failed. One has status four oh three and the other four oh one. Save the first finding, then trim off its source ID. Tomorrow's investigator gets only the sentence. Which record can the application fetch?

Try the lookup. The application has no key for the archive. Compacting that same sentence again won’t bring the key back. This is how an agent can spend several turns preparing its context without completing one investigation step. Cap those attempts and record the gap.

Recover the original checked note and pin its source ID. Try the same lookup again. There’s the callback and its four oh three. The stored note bought us a way back to the evidence. We can leave the full export in the archive and use the next call to inspect the failing dependency.

title: What survives the restart?

beats.say: One more shift takes over the investigation. After reserves, it has twenty-six hundred units for records. The task, trace and approval policy are all required. The old export ranks ahead of the current runbook. Use the sizes on screen. Which optional record fits alongside all three required records?

Pack the required records first. Together they use one thousand units. Try the old export. That would take twenty-eight hundred. Skip it and keep going. The runbook brings the total to twenty-two hundred, leaving four hundred free.

Open the saved collection receipt. Under Saved are the first digits of the hashes the evaluator checked. Under Current are the fingerprints of the files on disk. The harness compares every digit. Watch the report as a new revision of the trace arrives.

The report stays exactly as it was. The trace has a new revision. That trace can follow the stable prefix in a cacheable request. Look at the two fingerprints for the trace. Can the old receipt still certify collection?

Stop. The trace fingerprint changed. Reopen the revised trace and check the report against it. Read the request ID and status on each. Both say R seventeen, four oh three. The evaluator issues a fresh receipt for the report, the revised trace and the approval policy.
Now a summary leaves one required record out of the next call. The receipt still matches the files on disk. Which file would tell the model who can approve a rollback?

Read the approval policy back into this call. It names the incident lead. Now we know who can approve a rollback. In the next lesson, we’ll decide what to do when a document gives the agent an instruction. The next ready task is to verify the cause.

Request R seventeen returned four oh three on the callback. The lock check ruled out one explanation. To verify a cause, compare the scope the callback needed with the scope the deployment actually granted.
